title: Clack, Clack, Ding!
sub: PreK–Kindergarten · The typewriter and its keys
objective: Children will listen to the sounds of writing tools, look closely at a typewriter’s round keys and find letters on them, and act out how a typewriter works. They will meet the exhibition’s big idea in a child’s words: long ago only a few people could write, and new tools helped many more people write and share their ideas.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Long ago, only a few people could write. Machines like the typewriter helped many more people write and share their ideas.

items.text: listen to the sounds of writing tools and pick out the typewriter
items.question: pick out the typewriter’s sound?
items.screen: hear the typewriter’s clack and ding

items.text: find letters on a typewriter’s keys, and the four letters of *TYPE* on the top row
items.question: find T, Y, P and E on the keys?
items.screen: find T, Y, P and E on the keys

items.text: say how a typewriter works: press a key, hear the bell, push the carriage back
items.question: say how a typewriter works?

materials: The Typing Station on a screen, with the sound on
The *Show your class* page (page 3), projected or printed
A pencil and a sheet of paper
questions: Which sound was the typewriter? How did you know?
What letter is on this key? Can you find a letter from your name?
When does the typewriter’s bell ring? What do you do then?
Who would you write a message to? What would it say?
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** the display case holds a portable Smith-Corona Galaxie typewriter and an Apple iMac G3, side by side. Which one is the typewriter? Which one has a screen?
**Virtual visit:** at the Typing Station, children can type on the typewriter, hear the bell and push the carriage back.

steps.title: What is making that sound?
script: Write a word with a pencil while the children watch. *“People write with other tools too. Close your eyes and listen.”* Play the three sounds one at a time: a quill pen, a typewriter, a computer keyboard. After each, ask: *“What is making that sound?”* Then tell them. *“Long, long ago, only a few people could write. Then people made machines to help many more people write. Today we meet one of them: the typewriter.”*

clips.label: A quill pen
clips.credit: “Quill pen writing on hard paper various speed” by freesound_community (Pixabay)

steps.purpose: Wonder at the sounds before naming the tools: writing can scratch, clack and tap.

steps.title: Round keys
script: Show the typewriter on page 3, the Urania from the exhibition’s posters. Let the children look first, then ask: *“What can you see?”* Point to the round keys, each with a silver rim and a letter on top: each key makes one letter. Invite children to name a letter they know.

screen.alt: A black Urania portable typewriter seen from the front: four rows of round silver-rimmed keys, the name Urania in gold above them and Clemens Müller A.G. Dresden in gold along the base
screen.caption: The Urania typewriter, from the exhibition’s posters

steps.purpose: Look before being told: a typewriter is rows of keys, and every key is a letter.
students: Point to a key. What letter is on it?

steps.title: Find T, Y, P, E
script: Then show the top row of the keyboard on page 3, the row that starts Q, W, E, R, T, Y. Find **T**, **Y**, **P** and **E** together. *“All four live in the same row. Put them together and they spell TYPE!”*

screen.text: Q  W  E  R  T  Y  U  I  O  P

steps.purpose: Find four letters in one row, and read the word they make.
students: Find T, Y, P and E.

steps.title: Be a typewriter
script: Open the Typing Station with the sound on and type *TYPE* on its typewriter, slowly, so the children see each letter land on the paper. Keep typing until the bell rings near the end of the line: *ding!* Then press the carriage return, and the paper moves up to a new line.

Now everyone is a typewriter. Tap your fingers on your knees: *clack, clack, clack.* Lean as the line runs out, call *“Ding!”* together, and push the carriage back with one big sweep of the arm: *swoosh!* Play it two or three times.

screen.alt: The Typing Station room: a typewriter on the coral wall, its first line typed on the sheet of paper, with the tabs Typewriter, iMac, Top row and Class Board
screen.caption: The Typing Station: a typewriter and an iMac

steps.purpose: See and hear a typewriter at work, then act it out with the whole body.

steps.title: Your handout
script: Each child works on a handout. All three have the same keys and the same word: TYPE.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Picture-led. Look at the typewriter’s round keys, find and color T, Y, P and E on the top row, trace *TYPE*, and draw a picture message.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: A little writing. Find and color T, Y, P and E, copy *TYPE* under a model, circle the letter their name begins with, and draw who they would write to.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Draw and tell. Number the letters of TYPE in order, put the typewriter’s clack, ding and swoosh in order, then draw a message and say who would read it.

steps.purpose: Find, color and trace the letters at the right level for each child.
students: Find T, Y, P and E on your page.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the questions on the screen. For each one, the children show a thumb up, sideways or down: *“Can you now pick out the typewriter’s sound? Can you find T, Y, P and E on the keys? Can you say how a typewriter works?”*

screen.hint: Show me: thumb up, sideways or down.

steps.purpose: Check what each child can now do against the objectives.
students: find T, Y, P and E on the keys?

steps.title: Look back and share
script: Then say: *“Long ago, only a few people could write. Now you can! Tell a partner: if you could send a message to anyone, who would it be for?”*

screen.question: Long ago, only a few people could write. Now you can! Tell a partner: if you could send a message to anyone, who would it be for?

steps.purpose: End with the big idea: everyone can write now, and writing is for someone.
students: Tell a partner: who would your message be for?
